subject: Physics
stem: In a Vernier callipers, 20 vernier scale divisions is equal to 19 main scale divisions and there are 20 divisions per cm on the main scale. When a sphere is placed between the jaws of the Vernier callipers, the main scale reading is 2.5 mm and Vernier coinciding division is 4. Find the radius of the sphere.
solution:
\(1\text{ MSD} = \frac{1}{20}\text{ cm} = 0.5\text{ mm}\). Since 20 VSD = 19 MSD, \(\text{LC} = 1\text{ MSD} - 1\text{ VSD} = \frac{1\text{ MSD}}{20} = \frac{0.5}{20}\text{ mm} = 0.025\text{ mm}\).
Diameter \(= \text{MSR} + (\text{VC} \times \text{LC}) = 2.5 + 4 \times 0.025 = 2.6\text{ mm}\).
Radius \(= \frac{2.6}{2} = 1.3\text{ mm}\).

subject: Physics
stem:
The possible errors in using the screw gauge and Vernier callipers is
A) parallax error
B) random error
C) zero error
D) end correction error
solution: Both instruments can show a zero error, when the zero marks do not coincide with the jaws closed. Both are also read against a scale, so a reading taken at an angle gives a parallax error. End correction belongs to experiments such as the resonance tube and the metre bridge, not to these instruments. So the errors are A (parallax) and C (zero error).

subject: Physics
stem: In an instrument, there are 25 divisions on the vernier scale which coincides with 24 divisions of the main scale. 1 cm on main scale is divided into 20 equal parts. The least count of the instrument is
solution:
25 VSD = 24 MSD, so \(1\text{ VSD} = \frac{24}{25}\text{ MSD}\).
\(\text{LC} = 1\text{ MSD} - 1\text{ VSD} = \frac{1}{25}\text{ MSD}\).
With \(1\text{ MSD} = \frac{1}{20}\text{ cm}\): \(\text{LC} = \frac{1}{25} \times \frac{1}{20}\text{ cm} = \frac{1}{500}\text{ cm} = 0.002\text{ cm}\).
reasoning: The book's own solution ends with '= 0.02 cm', an arithmetic slip (1/500 = 0.002). Its key, option 1 (0.002 cm), is right; the solution here is corrected.

subject: Physics
stem:
**Statement I:** In Vernier callipers, if zero of Vernier scale lies to the right of zero of main scale, without any object kept between jaws, Vernier scale coincidence must be counted from left on Vernier scale.
**Statement II:** If zero of Vernier scale lies to the left of zero of main scale when jaws are in contact, Vernier scale coincidence must be counted from right on Vernier scale.
options: statements I and II are correct
statements I and II are false
statement I is correct and statement II is false
statement I is false and statement II is correct
solution: Vernier zero to the right of the main-scale zero is a positive zero error: it equals the coinciding division counted from the left (from the vernier zero) times the least count. Vernier zero to the left is a negative zero error: the coinciding division is counted from the right end of the vernier, \(\text{ZE} = -(N - n) \times \text{LC}\). Both statements are correct.

subject: Physics
stem: What is the least count of the Vernier callipers?
options: smallest division on the vernier scale
difference of the smallest division on the main scale and smallest division on the vernier scale
sum of the smallest division on the main scale and the smallest division on the vernier scale
smallest division on the main scale
solution: Least count = 1 MSD - 1 VSD. For example, if 10 VSD = 9 MSD, then \(1\text{ VSD} = \frac{9}{10}\text{ MSD}\) and \(\text{LC} = 1\text{ MSD} - 1\text{ VSD} = \frac{1}{10}\text{ MSD}\): the difference between one main-scale division and one vernier division.

subject: Physics
stem: If observed reading is OR, corrected reading is CR, zero error is ZE and zero correction is ZC then what will be the possibility?
solution:
Corrected reading = observed reading - zero error: \(\text{CR} = \text{OR} - \text{ZE}\).
Zero correction is the negative of zero error, \(\text{ZC} = -\text{ZE}\), so \(\text{CR} = \text{OR} + \text{ZC}\), i.e. \(\text{ZC} = \text{CR} - \text{OR}\).
Only option (4) has both relations right.

subject: Physics
stem: The n divisions of main scale coincides with (n + 1) divisions of Vernier scale. Given one main scale division is equal to 'a' units. Find the least count of the Vernier calliper.
solution:
(n + 1) VSD = n MSD, so \(1\text{ VSD} = \frac{n}{n+1}\text{ MSD}\).
\(\text{LC} = 1\text{ MSD} - 1\text{ VSD} = \left(1 - \frac{n}{n+1}\right)\text{MSD} = \frac{1}{n+1}\text{ MSD} = \frac{a}{n+1}\).

subject: Physics
stem: If the zero mark on the vernier scale lies towards the left side of the zero mark of the main scale, when the jaws are closed, then what will be the zero error?
solution: With the jaws closed the reading should be zero. If the vernier zero lies to the left of the main-scale zero, the instrument reads less than the true value, so the zero error is negative.

subject: Physics
stem: The least count of a screw gauge is 0.005 mm and it has 100 equal divisions on its head scale, then the distance between two consecutive threads on its screw is
solution:
The distance between consecutive threads is the pitch.
\(\text{Pitch} = \text{LC} \times N = 0.005 \times 100 = 0.5\text{ mm}\).

subject: Physics
stem: The circular scale of a screw gauge has 200 divisions. When it is given 4 complete rotations, it moves through 2 mm. The least count of the screw gauge is
solution:
\(\text{Pitch} = \frac{2\text{ mm}}{4} = 0.5\text{ mm}\).
\(\text{LC} = \frac{\text{pitch}}{N} = \frac{0.5}{200}\text{ mm} = 2.5 \times 10^{-3}\text{ mm}\).

subject: Physics
stem: A screw gauge has least count of 0.01 mm and there are 50 divisions in its circular scale. The pitch of the screw gauge is
solution: \(\text{LC} = \frac{\text{pitch}}{N} \Rightarrow \text{pitch} = \text{LC} \times N = 0.01 \times 50 = 0.5\text{ mm}\).

subject: Physics
stem: When the screw and stud touch each other, the edges of a certain screw gauge is on left of the 0 mark on the main scale and the 96th division of the circular scale coincides with the circular line of graduation then what is the value of the zero error?
solution:
The edge of the circular scale is to the left of the zero mark, so the zero error is negative. Taking the usual 100-division head with least count 0.01 mm, the 96th division on the reference line means the screw is \(100 - 96 = 4\) divisions short of zero:
\(\text{ZE} = -(100 - 96) \times 0.01 = -0.04\text{ mm}\).
reasoning: The stem does not state the least count; the key (and the book's solution) assume a 100-division head with LC 0.01 mm.

subject: Physics
stem: A student measured the thickness of a metal sheet using a screw gauge with least count 0.001 cm and listed the measurements. The correct measurement is
solution: A reading is recorded to the least count of the instrument. With LC = 0.001 cm the reading has three decimal places: 4.220 cm.

subject: Physics
stem:
Given below are two statements:
**Statement I:** Least count of a screw gauge is directly proportional to the number of divisions on circular scale.
**Statement II:** A screw gauge having a smaller value of pitch has greater accuracy.
In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below.
options: Both statement I and statement II are correct
statement I is correct and statement II is incorrect
statement I is incorrect and statement II is correct
Both statements I and statement II are incorrect
solution:
\(\text{LC} = \frac{\text{pitch}}{N}\), so the least count is inversely proportional to N: Statement I is false.
A smaller pitch gives a smaller least count, and hence greater accuracy: Statement II is true.

subject: Physics
stem: The pitch scale of a screw gauge has 20 divisions per centimeter and the least count of the screw gauge is 0.01 mm. The number of divisions on the circular scale are
solution:
\(\text{Pitch} = \frac{1\text{ cm}}{20} = 0.5\text{ mm}\).
\(N = \frac{\text{pitch}}{\text{LC}} = \frac{0.5}{0.01} = 50\).

subject: Physics
stem:
The circular scale of a screw gauge has 50 divisions and pitch of 0.5 mm. Find the diameter of sphere. (Main scale reading is 2 divisions)

In the figure, the circular-scale division on the reference line is 5 with the jaws closed (left) and 25 with the sphere between the jaws (right).
solution:
\(\text{LC} = \frac{0.5}{50} = 0.01\text{ mm}\).
With the jaws closed the circular scale reads 5 divisions: a zero error of \(+5 \times 0.01 = +0.05\text{ mm}\).
With the sphere, MSR = 2 divisions = \(2 \times 0.5 = 1.00\text{ mm}\) and the circular scale reads 25.
Diameter \(= 1.00 + (25 - 5)(0.01) = 1.00 + 0.20 = 1.20\text{ mm}\).

subject: Physics
stem:
**Assertion:** A screw gauge having smaller pitch has smaller least count.
**Reason:** Least count is directly proportional to number of circular divisions
options: Both assertion and reason are true and reason is correct explanation of assertion
Both assertion and reason are true but reason is not the correct explanation
Assertion is true and reason is false
Assertion is false but reason is true
solution: \(\text{LC} = \frac{\text{pitch}}{N}\). A smaller pitch gives a smaller least count, so the assertion is true. The least count is inversely (not directly) proportional to the number of circular divisions, so the reason is false.

subject: Physics
stem:
I. Screw gauge works on the principle of micrometer screw.
II. To avoid backlash error, the screw is well greased and is always turned in the same direction while taking observations.
options: I is correct, II is false
I is false, II is correct
solution: A screw gauge is a micrometer screw: the screw advances one pitch per rotation, and the fraction of a rotation is read on the circular scale. Backlash comes from play between the screw and the nut, so the screw is kept greased and always turned in one direction. Both statements are correct.

subject: Physics
stem: The diameter of a spherical ball is measured using first with Vernier scale and next with a screw gauge. Generally which measurement will have more possible error in measurement in the laboratory.
options: depends on the size of spherical ball
solution: The possible error is set by the least count: about 0.1 mm for Vernier callipers against 0.01 mm for a screw gauge. So the Vernier measurement carries the larger possible error.

subject: Physics
stem: Using the ratchet of screw gauge, the screw should be rotated in same direction to avoid
solution: Turning the screw only one way (through the ratchet) keeps the screw pressed against the same face of the nut thread, so the play between them, the backlash error, does not enter the reading.

subject: Physics
stem: To calculate the effective length of pendulum, we measure
options: length of string with metre scale and diameter of bob with Vernier callipers
distance between point of suspension and top of bob with metre scale.
distance between point of suspension and bottom of bob with metre scale.
distance between point of suspension and top of bob by metre scale and add half of diameter of bob, measured with Vernier callipers.
solution: The effective length runs from the point of suspension to the centre of the bob. Measure the length up to the top of the bob with a metre scale, then add the bob's radius: half its diameter, measured with Vernier callipers.

subject: Physics
stem: Damping force acting on a simple pendulum is proportional to
solution: \(F_d = -bv\): the damping force is proportional to the velocity and acts opposite to it.

subject: Physics
stem: In a damped oscillation of a pendulum
options: the sum of potential energy and kinetic energy is conserved
solution: The damping force does negative work, so the mechanical energy (KE + PE) is gradually lost as heat. Mechanical energy is not conserved.

subject: Physics
stem: In a damped oscillation with damping constant b, the time taken for amplitude of oscillation to drop to half what is its initial value?
solution:
\(A = A_0 e^{-bt/2m}\). Setting \(A = \frac{A_0}{2}\):
\(\frac{1}{2} = e^{-bt/2m} \Rightarrow \frac{bt}{2m} = \log 2 \Rightarrow t = \frac{2m}{b}\log 2\) (natural logarithm).

subject: Physics
stem:
**Assertion:** The amplitude of oscillation decreases exponentially with time, when a pendulum is oscillating in a viscous medium.
**Reason:** While moving in a viscous medium, energy is spent to move and hence amplitude decreases.
options: Both assertion and reason are correct and reason is the correct explanation of the assertion
Both assertion and reason are correct but reason is not the correct explanation of the assertion
Assertion is correct, but reason is incorrect
Assertion is incorrect but reason is correct
solution: In a viscous medium the pendulum does work against the drag, so its energy falls and the amplitude decays as \(A = A_0 e^{-bt/2m}\). Since \(E = \frac{1}{2}kA^2\), the energy decays as \(E = \frac{1}{2}kA_0^2 e^{-bt/m}\). The reason correctly explains the assertion.

subject: Physics
subtopic: Metre Scale and Balances (Principle of Moments)
stem: In the scale and fulcrum experiment, 'm' situated at 'x' from the fulcrum and M is situated at 'y' from fulcrum at equilibrium. Now if m < M, then what is the relation between x and y.
options: nothing can be said about x and y unless values m and M are known
solution: Balancing moments about the fulcrum: \(mgx = Mgy \Rightarrow \frac{x}{y} = \frac{M}{m}\). With \(m < M\), \(x > y\).

subject: Physics
subtopic: Metre Scale and Balances (Principle of Moments)
stem: If a uniform metre scale (beam) is used to find the mass of an unknown body and maintained in equilibrium about its midpoint, then the known and unknown masses should be
options: on either side of midpoint of scale
on the same side of midpoint
depending on the shape of masses
solution: For equilibrium about the midpoint the two moments must act in opposite senses, \(m_1 d_1 = m_2 d_2\), so the masses hang on either side of the midpoint.

subject: Physics
subtopic: Metre Scale and Balances (Principle of Moments)
stem: If the fulcrum is at other than midpoint of a uniform horizontal beam is used to measure an unknown weight 'W'. The balancing weights are \(W_1\) and \(W_2\) when the unknown weight is suspended at the ends of longer arm and shorter arm, then W is equal to
solution:
Let the arms be \(d_1\) and \(d_2\). With W on one arm: \(Wd_1 = W_1d_2\). With W on the other arm: \(Wd_2 = W_2d_1\).
Multiplying, \(W^2d_1d_2 = W_1W_2d_1d_2\), so \(W = \sqrt{W_1W_2}\).
reasoning: Like the book's solution, treats the beam's own weight as balanced (negligible).

subject: Physics
stem: A solid cylindrical steel column is 4 m long and 9 cm in diameter. (\(Y_{\text{steel}} = 1.9 \times 10^{10}\,\text{N/m}^2\)). The decrease in length of the column, while carrying a load of 80000 N is
solution:
\(Y = \frac{FL}{A\,\Delta L} \Rightarrow \Delta L = \frac{FL}{AY}\).
\(A = \pi r^2 = \pi (0.045)^2 = 6.36 \times 10^{-3}\text{ m}^2\).
\(\Delta L = \frac{80000 \times 4}{6.36 \times 10^{-3} \times 1.9 \times 10^{10}} = 2.65 \times 10^{-3}\text{ m} \approx 2.6\text{ mm}\).

subject: Physics
stem: In Searle's apparatus dead load is attached to both wires, before starting experiment to measure extension the reason is
options: to make the wires hang straight without any kinks
solution: The initial dead load keeps both wires taut and free of kinks, so the extension measured afterwards is the true elastic elongation of a straight wire.

subject: Physics
stem:
**Assertion:** In Searle's apparatus, experimental wire and reference wire must be made of same material and should have same length and may or may not have same radius of cross section.
**Reason:** If any temperature changes in the surrounding, both will equally change in their length.
options: Both assertion and reason are correct and reason is the correct explanation of the assertion
Both assertion and reason are correct but reason is not the correct explanation of the assertion
Assertion is correct, but reason is incorrect
Assertion is incorrect but reason is correct
solution: The reference wire cancels changes that are not due to the load. If both wires are of the same material and length, a change in room temperature changes both lengths equally, and the spirit-level reading is unaffected. The reason correctly explains the assertion.

subject: Physics
stem: The amount of energy evolved when eight droplets of mercury (surface tension 0.55 N/m) of radius 1 mm each combine into one drop is
solution:
Volume is conserved: \(\frac{4}{3}\pi R^3 = 8 \times \frac{4}{3}\pi r^3 \Rightarrow R = 8^{1/3}r = 2r = 2 \times 10^{-3}\text{ m}\).
Energy released \(= T\,\Delta A = T \cdot 4\pi(8r^2 - R^2) = 0.55 \times 4 \times 3.14 \times (8 \times 10^{-6} - 4 \times 10^{-6})\)
\(= 0.55 \times 4 \times 3.14 \times 4 \times 10^{-6} = 27.6 \times 10^{-6}\text{ J} \approx 28\,\mu\text{J}\).

subject: Physics
stem: The height of liquid raised into vertically dipped capillary tube, above free surface of liquid, does not depend on
options: the length of capillary tube dipped inside the liquid
solution: \(h = \frac{2T\cos\theta}{r\rho g}\). The rise depends on the radius, and on the surface tension, which changes with temperature and with impurities. It does not depend on how much of the tube is dipped in the liquid.

subject: Physics
stem: When the water rises into a vertically dipped capillary glass tube, the correct diagram indicating capillary is (see diagrams 1 to 4 in the figure)
options: Diagram 1: the water surface in the tube is flat
Diagram 2: the water surface in the tube is convex (bulging upward)
Diagram 3: the water surface in the tube is concave (dipping at the centre)
Diagram 4: the level in the tube is below the outside level, with a convex surface
solution: Water wets glass (its angle of contact is less than \(90^\circ\)), so it rises in the tube and its surface is concave upward: the meniscus dips at the centre. That is diagram 3.
reasoning: The book's options are the four diagrams; the option text describes each one so the question still reads without the figure.

subject: Physics
stem: The instrument used to measure height of water raised into glass capillary tube in the laboratory is
options: A Vernier callipers attached to a travelling microscope
Screw gauge attached to travelling microscope
solution: The capillary rise is read with a travelling microscope, whose vertical movement is measured on a vernier scale. The microscope is focused on the meniscus and then on the outside water level, and the difference of the two vernier readings gives h.

subject: Physics
stem: For more accurate measurement of terminal velocity in a viscous liquid the radius of spherical body to be selected is of
options: More radius and more density than that of liquid
Less radius and less density than that of liquid
less radius and more density than that of liquid
more radius and less density than that of liquid
solution: The ball must be denser than the liquid, or it will not sink. A small radius keeps the terminal velocity \(v = \frac{2r^2(\rho - \sigma)g}{9\eta}\) low, so the fall is slow enough to time accurately.

subject: Physics
stem:
**Assertion:** The free fall of spherical body through viscous liquid must be in the middle of vessel.
**Reason:** The velocity of free fall is affected by the nearness of the walls of vessel.
options: Both assertion and reason are correct and reason is the correct explanation of the assertion
Both assertion and reason are correct but reason is not the correct explanation of the assertion
Assertion is correct, but reason is incorrect
Assertion is incorrect but reason is correct
solution: Near the walls the drag on the ball increases (the wall effect), which lowers its velocity. So the ball is dropped along the axis of the vessel, and the reason explains the assertion.

subject: Physics
stem: In resonating air column experiment a student used a tuning fork of 510 Hz and found first resonating length at 17 cm. If the student next uses a fork of 480 Hz, he should try for first resonating air column length are
solution: For a fixed speed of sound, \(l_1 \approx \frac{v}{4f}\), so the resonating length is inversely proportional to the frequency. A lower frequency (480 Hz) gives a first resonance above 17 cm, about \(17 \times \frac{510}{480} \approx 18\text{ cm}\).

subject: Physics
stem:
**Statement I:** Always an antinode is formed at open end and node is formed at closed end of resonating air column.
**Statement II:** While finding speed of sound in resonating air column experiment, position of second resonance is also found to eliminate end correction measurement.
options: statements I and II are correct
statements I and II are false
statement I is correct and II is false
statement I is false and II is correct
solution: At the closed end the air cannot move (a node); at the open end it moves freely (an antinode, just beyond the end). With the first two resonances, \(l_1 + e = \frac{\lambda}{4}\) and \(l_2 + e = \frac{3\lambda}{4}\), so \(v = 2f(l_2 - l_1)\) and the end correction e cancels. Both statements are correct.

subject: Physics
stem:
**Statement I:** Temperature of liquid and solid in calorimeter is to be measured after stirring the mixture thoroughly only.
**Statement II:** The calorimeter along with its contents (hot + cold mixture) is kept in a wooden box containing non-conducting material like cotton, while measuring temperature.
options: statements I and II are correct
statements I and II are false
statement I is correct and II is false
statement I is false and II is correct
solution: Stirring brings the mixture to one uniform temperature before it is read, and the insulated wooden box cuts heat exchange with the surroundings. Both are correct precautions.

subject: Physics
stem: Two liquids of equal volume are thoroughly mixed. If their specific heats are \(c_1, c_2\), temperatures \(\theta_1, \theta_2\) and densities \(d_1, d_2\) respectively, what is the final temperature of the mixture?
solution:
Equal volumes V, so the masses are \(Vd_1\) and \(Vd_2\). Heat lost = heat gained:
\(Vd_1c_1(\theta_1 - \theta_0) = Vd_2c_2(\theta_0 - \theta_2)\)
\(d_1c_1\theta_1 + d_2c_2\theta_2 = \theta_0(d_1c_1 + d_2c_2) \Rightarrow \theta_0 = \frac{d_1c_1\theta_1 + d_2c_2\theta_2}{d_1c_1 + d_2c_2}\).

subject: Physics
stem: The hot solid is to be transferred quickly into calorimeter with water, without splash of water from calorimeter. The reason for above case is
options: to minimize loss of heat to surroundings and to keep mass of measured water to be same
solution: A quick transfer limits the heat the solid loses to the air on the way, and avoiding a splash keeps the measured mass of water unchanged. Both quantities enter the heat balance.

subject: Physics
subtopic: Metre Scale and Balances (Principle of Moments)
stem: A false balance has equal arms. An object weighs 'x' when placed in one pan and 'y' when placed in the other pan. The true weight 'W' of the object is
solution:
The arms are equal (\(\ell\)) but the pans weigh \(W_1\) and \(W_2\). Balancing:
\((W + W_1)\ell = (x + W_2)\ell\) and \((W + W_2)\ell = (y + W_1)\ell\).
Adding, \(2W = x + y\), so \(W = \frac{x+y}{2}\). (Unequal arms would give \(\sqrt{xy}\) instead.)

subject: Physics
stem: What is the resistance of an open key?
options: depends on the other resistance in the circuit
solution: An open key passes no current (\(i = 0\)) whatever the voltage across it, so \(R = \frac{V}{i} = \frac{V}{0} \to \infty\).

subject: Physics
stem: In electrical circuit connections connecting wires are rubbed with sand paper at their ends
options: To obtain electric contact, by erasing insulated coating
solution: Sand paper removes the insulating enamel and the oxide layer from the wire ends, so the connection makes good electrical contact.
reasoning: The book prints 'same paper'; its own solution says 'sand paper', so the stem reads 'sand paper'.

subject: Physics
stem: Which of following is incorrect?
options: The plug key should be inserted only when observations are to be taken
the balancing point will be obtained on the wire length, if the galvanometer shows deflecting in opposite sides, when jockey is touched at the ends of meter bridge wire.
with the change in the current allowed into the circuit, the balancing length also changes
jockey must be dragged along the metre bridge wire to find balancing point.
solution:
**Note:** As printed, this question has two incorrect statements. Option (3) is incorrect too: the balance condition \(\frac{R}{S} = \frac{l}{100 - l}\) contains no current, so the balancing length does not change with the current. The book's key, option (4), is kept.

The jockey must not be dragged along the wire: that scrapes the wire and spoils its uniform cross-section. It is pressed lightly at different points to find the balance point.
reasoning: Defective as printed (two incorrect options); key 4 kept with a notice, per the 2026-10-29 defective-question policy.

subject: Physics
stem: In the experiment to find the focal length of convex mirror by parallax method using converging lens. The image formed by converging lens is
solution: The convex lens forms a real image of the object pin, and the convex mirror is placed in the path of the rays converging to that image. The object pin is placed between f and 2f of the lens, so this real image is inverted and magnified, far enough behind the lens to leave room for the mirror.
reasoning: The book gives only 'Conceptual'; 'magnified' follows from the usual set-up with the object between f and 2f.

subject: Physics
stem: In parallax method, to find coincidence of image formed with the image formed by other lens (or) with object.
options: It must be observed with one eye closing the other eye and position of image must be confirmed by moving the eye either side such that image moves opposite to motion of eye.
It must be observed with both eyes opened
It must be observed with a specially prepared spectacle.
It must be observed using a polarizer.
solution: Parallax is judged with one eye. Move the eye from side to side and watch for relative motion between the image and the pin. When they move together, with no relative shift, they coincide.

subject: Physics
stem: In experiment finding focal length of a convex lens in the laboratory.
options: the object needle is to be kept at focus F
the object needle is to be kept at infinity
the object needle is to be kept at 2F and on either side to it
the object needle is to be kept at pole of lens
solution: To get a real, inverted image that can be located with an image needle, the object needle is placed around 2F, and on either side of it. At F the image goes to infinity, and at the lens itself no real image forms.

subject: Physics
stem: The minimum distance between an object and its real image formed by a convex lens of focal length 'f' is
solution: With object and image distances u and v (magnitudes), \(\frac{1}{u} + \frac{1}{v} = \frac{1}{f}\) and \(u + v = x\), so \(uv = fx\). Real u and v need \(x^2 \ge 4uv = 4fx\), i.e. \(x \ge 4f\). The minimum, 4f, is reached at \(u = v = 2f\).

subject: Physics
stem:
Keep the points in sequence order while doing the experiment for drawing i-d curve.
a) Trace the cross-section of prism
b) Draw the incident line on one face of prism
c) Draw normal to the refracting surface
d) Put the pins on the incident line drawn
e) Seeing through other refracting surface put two more pins at 1 cm gap in the same line and all 4 pins appear in the same line.
f) Measure angle of deviation between the extensions of incident and refracted lines.
solution: Trace the prism outline (a), draw the normal at the point of incidence (c), draw the incident ray at the chosen angle to that normal (b), fix two pins on it (d), fix two more pins in line with their images seen through the other face (e), then measure the deviation between the extended rays (f): a c b d e f.

subject: Physics
stem: The minimum deviation angle of a light ray for a given prism.
options: measured by taking average of deviations
measured by taking the minimum value measured from experiment
measured by drawing the free hand curve for i-d angles
by taking intersection of tangents drawn
solution: With pins, the exact minimum cannot be caught in a single reading. Deviation is measured for several angles of incidence, a smooth free-hand i-d curve is drawn through the points, and the lowest point of the curve gives the angle of minimum deviation.

subject: Physics
subtopic: Travelling Microscope (Refractive Index of a Glass Slab)
stem: After focusing the travelling microscope on the cross mark and after taking reading of its position, if a glass slab is kept on it, again to focus the cross mark.
options: microscope is to be moved upwards
microscope is to be moved downwards
microscope is to be moved leftwards
microscope is to be moved rightwards
solution: Seen through the slab, the cross mark appears raised to its apparent depth, so the microscope must be moved upward to refocus on it.

subject: Physics
subtopic: Travelling Microscope (Refractive Index of a Glass Slab)
stem: To determine refractive index of glass slab using a travelling microscope, minimum number of readings required are
solution:
Three readings: \(R_1\) on the mark without the slab, \(R_2\) on the mark seen through the slab, and \(R_3\) on the top surface of the slab. Then
\(\mu = \frac{\text{real depth}}{\text{apparent depth}} = \frac{R_3 - R_1}{R_3 - R_2}\).

subject: Physics
subtopic: Travelling Microscope (Refractive Index of a Glass Slab)
stem: The purpose of using Lycopodium powder,
options: To make the upper surface of glass slab to be focussed
solution: The glass surface is transparent and gives nothing to focus on. A thin sprinkle of lycopodium powder marks the top surface, so the microscope can be focused on it exactly.

subject: Physics
stem: In forward bias of PN junction diode the current is measured in the units of
solution: Forward current through a junction diode is of the order of milliamperes, so it is read on a milliammeter.

subject: Physics
stem: What is the resistance of the P-N junction diode in forward biasing?
solution: Forward biased, the depletion layer narrows and the diode conducts readily. Its resistance is low, a few ohms, but not zero.

subject: Physics
stem: Which of the following is an active component?
solution: An active component can deliver energy to a circuit, control the flow of current and produce power gain. A transistor does; resistors, capacitors and inductors are passive components.

subject: Physics
stem:
**Statement I:** Diode is a non-ohmic conductor.
**Statement II:** Though diode is non-ohmic conductor, the dynamic resistance of diode is measured as ratio of \(\frac{\Delta V}{\Delta i}\).
options: statement I is correct, II is incorrect
statement I is incorrect, II is correct
both statements I & II are correct
both statements I & II are incorrect
solution: A diode does not obey Ohm's law (its I-V graph is not a straight line), so it is non-ohmic. Its dynamic resistance at a point is \(r_d = \frac{\Delta V}{\Delta i}\). Both statements are correct.

subject: Physics
stem: In the zener diode, at \(V_Z\) breakdown voltage.
options: A small change in current causes a large change in voltage
A small change in current causes a small change in voltage
A large change in current produces an insignificant change in voltage
A large change in voltage produces an insignificant change in the current.
solution: At breakdown the zener's reverse current can change over a wide range while the voltage across it stays almost at \(V_Z\). This is why it is used as a voltage regulator.

subject: Physics
stem: In reverse bias of P-N junction diode the current is measured in the units of
solution: In reverse bias the current is carried by minority carriers only, so it is tiny, of the order of microamperes, and is read on a microammeter.

subject: Physics
stem: In the forward bias of PN junction diode, the current is zero, even though the potential applied is other than zero, the reason is
options: the applied potential is less than knee voltage of diode
the ammeter used is in reverse direction
unless it is tapped, ammeter will not show reading.
solution: Below the knee (cut-in) voltage, about 0.7 V for silicon, the applied voltage has not overcome the barrier potential, so the forward current is practically zero.

subject: Physics
stem: In the breakdown region, zener diode behaves as a
solution: In breakdown the voltage across the zener stays nearly constant at \(V_Z\) whatever the current, so it acts as a constant voltage source.

subject: Physics
stem: Which of the following is a three lead device?
solution: A transistor has three leads (emitter, base and collector). A diode, a resistor and a capacitor each have two.

subject: Physics
stem: Testing a good diode with a multimeter should indicate
options: high resistance when forward (or) reverse biased
low resistance when forward (or) reverse biased
high resistance when reverse biased and low resistance when forward biased
high resistance when forward biased and low resistance when reverse biased
solution: A good diode conducts one way only: low resistance when forward biased, high resistance when reverse biased.

subject: Physics
stem: Which of following does not conduct DC through it?
solution: Once charged, a capacitor blocks a steady (DC) current, because its dielectric does not conduct.

subject: Physics
stem: The P and N ends of a PN junction diode is found by
solution: A multimeter shows low resistance only when its positive lead is on the P side (forward bias), which identifies the P and N ends.
